name: Habitat for Humanity International: public awareness, education and housing advocacy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the global Home Equals campaign (98% of the result at the defaults), valued country by country over the 13 stand-in countries of the international build, each region a quarter of the people (Home Equals publishes no split, a judgment), so the shares follow each country's net value per person; US housing advocacy 2%.
summary: Habitat for Humanity International's (HFHI) public awareness and education programme ($24.3 million in the year to June 2025, plus an estimated $3.5 million of advocacy booked in its other programmes) runs Habitat's media, website and learning events and its housing-policy advocacy: in the US, where the Habitat network counts 142 policy wins and $6.65 billion of state and local housing money in FY2025 ($369 million in FY2026), and worldwide through the Home Equals campaign for informal settlements ($1.24 billion of government money and 7.9 million people since 2023, Habitat's counts). Built from the research on whether advocacy changes policy (most campaigns change nothing; organised constituent contact moves a legislator's vote by about 12 points), valuing the money as housing for the households it reaches net of what it costs the taxpayers who pay for it (with the cost of raising taxes), on the site's log-income scale, and with HFHI's small share of the coalitions behind the wins, a dollar does about 0.007 years of healthy life per $1,000, far below the global-health median. In the US the households helped are only modestly poorer per person than those who pay, so after programme costs and the housing's in-kind form the money gains almost nothing on that scale; 98% of the value is Home Equals', where the gap is wider. Both branches are discounted for missing data. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the money reaches households, how much poorer they are than those who pay, and how much of it the advocacy caused: across those ranges the result can be negative (the payers losing more than the households gain), which the site's log-scale range doesn't show.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.explainer: Habitat for Humanity International's (HFHI) third programme in its audited accounts, in US dollars (thousands in the statement): staff ($12.5 million), grants to Habitat organisations ($3.1 million), professional services ($3.5 million), donated media ($1.9 million) and office costs. The Form 990 describes it as sharing Habitat's message through media, habitat.org, social media and learning events; it also holds HFHI's housing-policy advocacy in the US (Habitat Voices in Action, which followed the Cost of Home campaign) and worldwide (Home Equals). Every dollar of it is counted as the cost of the policy wins below: the general awareness work has no outcome of its own beyond them (its effect on giving and volunteering is fundraising, already spread over the programmes as overhead, and volunteers' value is in the other models' attribution).

source.title: Habitat for Humanity, FY2025 annual report: Advocacy
source.page: Advocacy: 'Habitat advocates for public policies that expand pathways to affordable homeownership'
source.quote: unlocking more than US$6.65 billion in government funds for home affordability at the local and state levels
source.note: High end: FY2025 (this annual report). Low end: Habitat's figure for FY2026, 'US$369 million in government funds for home affordability accessed or allocated' (https://www.habitat.org/advocate/united-states/habitat-voices-in-action/advocacy-in-action, retrieved 2026-11-04). Best: their mean.

rows.explainer: Habitat's own count of the state and local government money for housing attached to the policy wins the US network supported (down-payment assistance funds, housing trust funds, repair programmes, budget lines). It swings eighteenfold from year to year with a few large budgets: $6.65 billion in FY2025, $369 million in FY2026. A year's spending buys a share of a lumpy stream of wins, so the best guess is the average of the two years since Cost of Home became Habitat Voices in Action, at about this level of spending: $3.51 billion; the range is the two years. Cost of Home's $23.6 billion over FY2020-24 is not used: it includes about $12 billion of federal pandemic relief, and the campaign's spending differed. How much of the money the wins caused is in us_counterfactual_adj; how much of the count is real and specific to the wins, in us_evidence_adj.

rows.explainer: The campaign's total as a yearly flow, about $590 million, against one year of the programme's cost.

rows.label: Home Equals: government money per person reached (US$)
rows.explainer: About $157 a person: informal-settlement upgrading (water, drainage, paths, tenure) spreads modest sums over many people.

rows.label: Home Equals: people reached by the money per year
rows.explainer: About 3.8 million a year, Habitat's own count.

rows.label: People reached by the money the year's policy wins opened up (both branches, Habitat's counts)
rows.explainer: For reading: the US and Home Equals branches together; each branch is valued at its own people's consumption.

rows.label: Money moved or raised for other charities in the year modelled (US$)
rows.explainer: 0: the programme moves no donations to other charities. Government money its advocacy helps win is valued in the policy branches above as what it does for the people it reaches, net of what it costs those who pay for it, not as money moved.

rows.label: Money moved per dollar of cost
rows.explainer: 0 here (no money moved).

rows.label: US: share of the government money that reaches households as housing
rows.explainer: State and local housing money passes through agencies, developers and lenders before it reaches households as down-payment help, repairs, rent or a cheaper home: administration, developer fees and units that go to households above the targets take a share. 0.8, range 0.6 to 0.95, the same order as the share of HFHI's own US programme that passes to affiliates as money and goods (65%) and of a cash charity's spending that reaches recipients (84%, GiveDirectly).

rows.label: US: years the housing the money buys keeps its value
rows.explainer: Down-payment help and new affordable homes last for the years the family stays (Habitat families mostly stay 15 years and more); repairs 10 to 25 years; rental help a year or two. 15, range 5 to 30. The result moves little with it: the money is spread over the same years it is discounted over.

rows.label: US: value reaching each person per year (US$)
rows.explainer: The money per person that reaches households, as an even yearly flow over the years it lasts (its present value equals the money at the shared discount rate).

rows.label: US: share of the people reached in the second-poorest fifth of incomes (the rest in the poorest)
rows.explainer: The programmes target households below 60% to 80% of the area's median income (Virginia's down-payment fund: 'earning no more than 60% of the area's median income'): down-payment and homebuilding money goes to working families in the second fifth, repair and rental money more to the poorest. 0.5, range 0.2 to 0.8.

rows.label: US: survey spending per person of the people reached, as a share of the survey mean
rows.explainer: The income fifths' household spending relative to the average household (BLS Consumer Expenditures 2024: poorest 0.446, second 0.637), put per person by each fifth's own household size (1.6 and 2.1 people, against 2.4 for all households: the shared facts): about 0.70 of the survey mean per person.

rows.label: US: consumption per person of the people reached (US$, household survey)
rows.explainer: The households' consumption by the household survey: us_recipient_share × the Consumer Expenditure Survey's $32,723 a person (2024). Changed 2026-11-04 (one rule for every model): a consumption baseline is the survey consumption of the people served, so the share of the gap to the national accounts' $58,517 that was spread over everyone is no longer added. A shared conversion, not thin data.

rows.label: US: what a dollar of housing help is worth to the household against a dollar of cash
rows.explainer: The same question and value as in Habitat's US model: studies of US housing assistance summarised by Olsen (2003, in Moffitt ed., Means-Tested Transfer Programs in the United States) find recipients value subsidised housing at less than its cost. 0.8, range 0.6 to 0.95.

rows.label: US: ln(consumption) gain per person reached, discounted
rows.formula: us_inkind_value * ln(1 + us_benefit_per_person_year / us_baseline_consumption) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, us_benefit_years)
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the households' own survey consumption, over the years the housing lasts, at its cash-equivalent value.

rows.label: US: how the taxes behind the money fall, relative to a tax proportional to consumption
rows.explainer: On the log scale a dollar taken from someone costs 1 over their consumption, so a tax proportional to true consumption costs 1 over the national-accounts mean (a multiple of 1); a progressive tax costs less (above 1), a regressive one more (below 1). The money is state and local: ITEP's Who Pays (7th edition, 2024) finds state and local taxes regressive against income (11.4% of income for the poorest fifth, 7.2% for the top 1%), but close to proportional against consumption, since poorer households consume more than their income. 1.05, range 0.75 (money taken from other programmes for poorer households, or regressive sales taxes) to 1.6 (federal or income-tax money).

rows.label: US: ln(consumption) given up by those who pay, per person reached
rows.explainer: Public money isn't free: the same dollars come from taxpayers or from other public spending. Spread thinly over many payers, each dollar costs them its share of their consumption (the log curve is straight for small amounts): the money per person, times the marginal cost of public funds, over the payers' consumption. So only the move of money from better-off payers to poorer households counts, as a transfer does on the log scale.

rows.label: US: net ln(consumption) gain per person reached
rows.explainer: The households' gain less the payers' loss.

rows.label: US: share of the money that is a lasting yearly stream rather than a one-off allocation
rows.explainer: Most of the wins Habitat lists are one-year appropriations (Virginia's $5 million for down-payment help, Asheville's $2.4 million after Hurricane Helene); some set up lasting streams (dedicated trust-fund revenue, permanent tax credits). 0.2, range 0.05 to 0.5.

rows.label: US: years the win's money is counted for, discounted
rows.explainer: A one-off allocation is counted once, after the wait; a lasting stream (a dedicated trust fund, a permanent programme) counts the site's years a won reform counts, discounted, like any won policy.

rows.label: US: value of the year's wins, before Habitat's share and adjustments (units of value)
rows.explainer: People reached × net log-consumption gain × the shared value of a doubled income × the years counted, times p_success (1: the wins happened), before the share the advocacy caused (the counterfactual, in the adjustments).

rows.label: US: households' gross value of the year's wins, before the payers' cost (units of value)
rows.explainer: The base for benefits and harms not modelled, which scale with what the households get, not with the net.

rows.label: Home Equals: share of the government money that reaches households as housing
rows.explainer: Government upgrading programmes for informal settlements (water, sanitation, drainage, paths, tenure, home improvement) lose more on the way to households than US programmes: administration, contractors, leakage and works that serve the wider city. 0.6, range 0.4 to 0.85.

rows.label: Home Equals: years the housing the money buys keeps its value
rows.explainer: Paths, drains, water connections and secure tenure last 10 to 25 years; small home improvements and emergency works a few years. 10, range 3 to 25. The result moves little with it.

rows.label: Home Equals: value reaching each person per year (US$)
rows.explainer: The money per person that reaches households, as an even yearly flow over the years it lasts (its present value equals the money at the shared discount rate).

rows.label: Home Equals: survey consumption of informal-settlement households, as a share of their country's survey mean
rows.explainer: Informal-settlement households are poorer than their countries' average but urban, and urban consumption is above rural: the bottom 40%'s survey consumption is 0.28 to 0.59 of the mean in the countries in he_cons_mean (World Bank SI.SPR.PC40 ÷ SI.SPR.PCAP, in facts/survey_consumption.json). And the average is over regions as different as Africa ($470) and Latin America ($3,100), so the range is wide: 0.5, range 0.25 to 0.9.

rows.label: Home Equals: consumption per person of the households reached (US$, averaged over the countries, for reading)
rows.formula: avg(avg(he_recipient_hnd, he_recipient_dom, he_recipient_per), avg(he_recipient_arm, he_recipient_mkd, he_recipient_rou, he_recipient_egy), avg(he_recipient_ken, he_recipient_uga, he_recipient_mwi, he_recipient_zmb), avg(he_recipient_phl, he_recipient_bgd))
rows.explainer: For reading: the countries' figures averaged as the branch's gain is (each region a quarter); the gain itself is taken country by country.

rows.label: Home Equals: what a dollar of housing help is worth to the household against a dollar of cash
rows.explainer: The same value as Habitat's international model gives its own incremental housing help (households would otherwise save for the same improvements, so in-kind help is close to its cash value: Cunha 2014, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, on Mexico's food transfers). 0.85, range 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Home Equals: ln(consumption) gain per person reached, discounted
rows.formula: avg(avg(he_gross_hnd, he_gross_dom, he_gross_per), avg(he_gross_arm, he_gross_mkd, he_gross_rou, he_gross_egy), avg(he_gross_ken, he_gross_uga, he_gross_mwi, he_gross_zmb), avg(he_gross_phl, he_gross_bgd))
rows.explainer: The households' gross gain, averaged over the countries (each region a quarter), each on the log curve at its own consumption.

rows.label: Home Equals: how the taxes behind the money fall, relative to a tax proportional to consumption
rows.explainer: Incidence only, as in the US branch (the payers' consumption level is the national-accounts mean, in he_net_<country>). Taxes in these countries are mostly consumption taxes, which are progressive in practice because poorer households buy more in informal markets that pay none: Bachas, Gadenne and Jensen (2024, Review of Economic Studies, 'Informality, consumption taxes, and redistribution') find effective consumption-tax rates rising with income across 31 countries. Part of the money is donors' and development banks' lending, repaid from the same taxes. 1.13, range 0.9 to 1.5.

rows.label: Home Equals: ln(consumption) given up by those who pay, per person reached
rows.formula: avg(avg(he_gross_hnd, he_gross_dom, he_gross_per), avg(he_gross_arm, he_gross_mkd, he_gross_rou, he_gross_egy), avg(he_gross_ken, he_gross_uga, he_gross_mwi, he_gross_zmb), avg(he_gross_phl, he_gross_bgd)) - avg(avg(he_net_hnd, he_net_dom, he_net_per), avg(he_net_arm, he_net_mkd, he_net_rou, he_net_egy), avg(he_net_ken, he_net_uga, he_net_mwi, he_net_zmb), avg(he_net_phl, he_net_bgd))
rows.explainer: For reading: the payers' cost per person reached, averaged over the countries (gross gain less net), each at its country's national-accounts mean.

rows.label: Home Equals: net ln(consumption) gain per person reached
rows.formula: avg(avg(he_net_hnd, he_net_dom, he_net_per), avg(he_net_arm, he_net_mkd, he_net_rou, he_net_egy), avg(he_net_ken, he_net_uga, he_net_mwi, he_net_zmb), avg(he_net_phl, he_net_bgd))
rows.explainer: The net gain averaged over the countries, each region a quarter, as in beneficiaries.

rows.label: Home Equals: share of the money that is a lasting yearly stream rather than a one-off allocation
rows.explainer: Mostly one-off programme budgets and loans for upgrading; a few lasting rules (land-tenure and building-code reforms carry no money and are in unmodelled_benefits_adj). 0.1, range 0 to 0.3.

rows.label: Home Equals: years the win's money is counted for, discounted
rows.explainer: A one-off allocation is counted once, after the wait; a lasting stream (a dedicated trust fund, a permanent programme) counts the site's years a won reform counts, discounted, like any won policy.

rows.label: Home Equals: value of the year's wins, before Habitat's share and adjustments (units of value)
rows.explainer: People reached × net log-consumption gain × the shared value of a doubled income × the years counted, times p_success (1: the wins happened), before the share the advocacy caused (the counterfactual, in the adjustments).

rows.label: Home Equals: households' gross value of the year's wins, before the payers' cost (units of value)
rows.explainer: The base for benefits and harms not modelled, which scale with what the households get, not with the net.

rows.label: Marginal cost of public funds: what a dollar of public money costs those who pay, in dollars
rows.explainer: Raising a dollar of tax costs the economy more than a dollar, through the work and spending it discourages: estimates for rich countries' taxes run from about 1.1 to 1.5 (Dahlby 2008, The Marginal Cost of Public Funds: Theory and Applications, MIT Press), and for African countries' taxes mostly 1.1 to 1.3 (Auriol and Warlters 2012, Journal of Development Economics, 38 countries). 1.2, range 1 (money shifted from other spending) to 1.5. Both branches.

rows.label: Net value per person reached, both branches (units of value, before the share the advocacy caused)
rows.formula: (us_people * us_net_ln_per_person * us_years_factor + he_people * he_net_ln_per_person * he_years_factor) * $uov_per_ln_consumption / units_affected_per_year
rows.explainer: For reading: the people-weighted net value per person, in units of value, over the years counted.

rows.label: Probability the wins happen, given the work
rows.explainer: 1: the model counts the policy wins of the year, which have happened (Habitat reports wins, not campaigns), against all the year's spending, the failed campaigns' included. Whether they would have come anyway is the counterfactual, in each branch's counterfactual_adj (Convention 5: one question, asked once).

rows.label: Years a won reform counts
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9), for the share of the money that is a lasting yearly stream.

rows.label: Wait from the win to when the money reaches households
rows.explainer: Appropriations reach households after the programme is set up and the first homes or grants are made: about a year (down-payment funds open within months; building programmes take two to three years).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Years a lasting win counts, discounted
rows.explainer: The site's years for a won reform, discounted at the shared rate, after the wait.

rows.label: Value of the year's policy wins, both branches (units of value, before Habitat's share)
rows.explainer: The two branches' value before the adjustments; each branch's own adjustments are applied in outcome_total.

rows.label: Value of the money moved (units of value)
rows.explainer: 0 here (no money moved); the shared rows are kept so the model reads like the family's others.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium's seasonal malaria chemoprevention, Helen Keller Intl's vitamin A, New Incentives), each at its result on this site under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: This organisation moves money only to global health and poverty charities, so a dollar moved is valued at that destination alone (GiveWell's Top Charities, live).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Careers changed to high-impact work in the year modelled
rows.explainer: 0: the programme doesn't move people into jobs.

rows.label: Pay a career changer gives up per year (US$)
rows.explainer: Unused (no careers changed); the template's placeholder range. Multiplied by careers_changed, 0.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays in high-impact work
rows.explainer: Unused (no careers changed); the template's placeholder range. Multiplied by careers_changed, 0.

rows.label: Share of the career changes the charity caused
rows.explainer: Unused (no careers changed); the template's placeholder range. Multiplied by careers_changed, 0.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays, discounted
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of the new employers' work (units of value)
rows.explainer: Unused (no careers changed): the moved-money destination value, as the template has it.

rows.label: Value of one career change (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one career-change step (docs/normalization.md 2.8).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step for career changes; unused here (no careers changed).

rows.label: Value of the career changes (units of value)
US: share of the money that wouldn't have come at all, or not for many years, without the advocacy coalitions Habitat was part of
rows.explainer: The research on whether advocacy changes policy: Baumgartner, Berry, Hojnacki, Kimball and Leech (2009, Lobbying and Policy Change, 98 random US federal issues) find about 60% of campaigns change nothing, the status quo usually wins and resources explain under 5% of who wins; field experiments find constituent contacts organised by an advocacy coalition raise a Michigan legislator's support for a bill by about 12 percentage points (Bergan and Cole 2015, Political Behavior; Bergan 2009 for e-mail lobbying), while lobbyists' policy information alone moved no votes in four experiments (Camp et al. 2023, Journal of Experimental Political Science). Habitat's count includes every win it supported, many of them in coalitions with the realtors, homebuilders and state housing alliances, where the advocacy as a whole was pivotal for a minority of the money. 0.15, range 0.03 to 0.4. This is the counterfactual: the share that would not have come at all, or not for many years, without the coalition's advocacy (money that would merely have come a year or two later is in the other 85%, and counts nothing, as Convention 5 asks: one question); Habitat's share of the coalition is in us_attribution_share; how much of the reported money is real, in us_evidence_adj.

rows.label: US: how much of Habitat's count of money and people is real and specific to the wins
rows.explainer: One question: how much of the money Habitat counts is real public money for the wins it lists, counted once. The figures are its network's self-reports with no published method: several affiliates can report the same state budget, and some money is a multi-year total reported in one year. (Whether the wins caused the money is the counterfactual; how lumpy the years are is in us_funds' range.) Habitat funded the Urban Institute to assess policy changes from Cost of Home's first four years, which published no check of the totals. 0.6, range 0.3 to 0.9.

rows.label: US: Habitat organisations' share of the resources of the coalitions behind the wins
rows.explainer: Habitat organisations are usually one member of state and local housing coalitions with realtors, homebuilders, state housing alliances, community land trusts and national groups (the National Low Income Housing Coalition, Enterprise, LISC; Cost of Home's endorsers included the Mortgage Bankers Association). On homeownership measures Habitat often leads (Virginia's down-payment fund, which it describes as its own campaign). 0.15, range 0.05 to 0.4.

rows.label: US: HFHI's share of the Habitat network's resources for this advocacy
rows.explainer: Within Habitat, local and state Habitat organisations do the advocacy that wins state and local money, with HFHI's staff, training and grants. In Cost of Home (FY2020-24) HFHI's campaign raised $6.8 million and Habitat organisations leveraged $23.7 million (the cumulative report's expenditure page, p. 18), so HFHI was about 22% of the campaign's money; HFHI's grants to affiliates ($2.3 million over five years) asked for match, and the affiliates' volunteers' unpaid advocacy is in neither figure. 0.2, range 0.1 to 0.4.

rows.label: US: HFHI's share of all the resources behind the wins
rows.explainer: Convention 2: the charity's share of everyone's resources behind the outcome, the coalition's partners and the Habitat network's own organisations and volunteers included.

rows.label: US: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for Habitat
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12): the reach is Habitat's own count, but what the advocacy changed and what the money did for the households are built from the research on advocacy and housing assistance and from judgment, not measured in an evaluation of Habitat's work (whether the money would have come anyway has its own row). The shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: US: adjustments combined
Home Equals: share of the money that wouldn't have come at all, or not for many years, without the advocacy coalitions Habitat was part of
rows.explainer: The research on whether advocacy changes policy: Baumgartner, Berry, Hojnacki, Kimball and Leech (2009, Lobbying and Policy Change, 98 random US federal issues) find about 60% of campaigns change nothing, the status quo usually wins and resources explain under 5% of who wins; field experiments find constituent contacts organised by an advocacy coalition raise a Michigan legislator's support for a bill by about 12 percentage points (Bergan and Cole 2015, Political Behavior; Bergan 2009 for e-mail lobbying), while lobbyists' policy information alone moved no votes in four experiments (Camp et al. 2023, Journal of Experimental Political Science). Global campaigns that count government money 'secured' for a broad cause (informal-settlement upgrading, which governments, UN-Habitat, the World Bank and slum-dweller federations all push) caused less of it than a state coalition behind one bill: 0.1, range 0.02 to 0.3.

rows.label: Home Equals: how much of Habitat's count of money and people is real and specific to the wins
rows.explainer: Habitat's global totals are national organisations' self-reports with no published method, for broad commitments ('government funding to improve housing in informal settlements'), some of them plans and loans not yet spent. One question, as in the US branch (how much is real money for the listed wins, counted once): 0.5, range 0.2 to 0.9.

rows.label: Home Equals: Habitat organisations' share of the resources of the coalitions behind the wins
rows.explainer: Home Equals is Habitat's campaign, and its national organisations often lead the country asks, but informal-settlement upgrading is also pushed by UN-Habitat, the World Bank, Slum Dwellers International and city governments themselves. 0.2, range 0.05 to 0.5.

rows.label: Home Equals: HFHI's share of the Habitat network's resources for this advocacy
rows.explainer: HFHI runs the campaign and its global policy staff; Habitat national organisations do most of the country advocacy with their own staff and donors. 0.4, range 0.2 to 0.7.

rows.label: Home Equals: HFHI's share of all the resources behind the wins
rows.explainer: Convention 2: the charity's share of everyone's resources behind the outcome, the coalition's partners and the Habitat network's own organisations and volunteers included.

rows.label: Home Equals: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for Habitat
rows.explainer: Thin: Habitat's own count of money and people, with the counterfactual and the value built from the research literature and judgment. The shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: Home Equals: adjustments combined
Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' adjustments, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of the money the advocacy caused (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' counterfactuals, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: HFHI's share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' shares, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of credit used (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared. Each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Missing-data step (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' missing-data steps, for reading only; both are thin, so this is the shared discount.

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' combined adjustments, for reading only; each branch applies its own in outcome_total.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the households' gross value
rows.explainer: Not modelled, as a share of the households' gross value (before the payers' cost): (+) wins that carry no money, such as land-use and zoning reforms (in US cities, loosening reforms raise the housing stock by about 0.8% within three to nine years, mostly at the upper end of the rent distribution: Stacy et al. 2023, Urban Studies) and land-tenure rules in Home Equals countries, +3%; (+) public attitudes to affordable housing from the awareness work, not measured, +1%; (−) wins that crowd out other housing spending, −1%. Range −5% to +15%.

rows.label: Total units of value
rows.formula: us_value * us_total_adj + he_value * he_total_adj + unmodelled_benefits_adj * (us_gross_value * us_total_adj + he_gross_value * he_total_adj) + moved_value + careers_value
rows.explainer: Each branch's net value times its own adjustments, plus what isn't modelled as a share of the households' gross value (so its sign doesn't flip when the net does); money moved and careers are 0. The result can be negative across the ranges: when the households gain less than the payers lose.

rows.explainer: The shared gap for communications and media staff (@staff_pay.gap_media, 20%): most of the programme's staff run Habitat's media, digital and events, in Atlanta; a few are policy staff in Washington (whose shared gap, gap_advocacy, is higher).

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: This model's cost per outcome is the charity's past spending over what it won (estimate_basis past_average), so the next dollar is valued at the shared share of the average (docs/normalization.md 2.10). 1 in `published`: what the past average itself says.

rows.label: Share of the full cost paid by cash donations
Units of value per dollar you give
rows.explainer: The year's wins over the year's spending, at the shared share of the average that the next dollar does (estimate_basis past_average).
